quote: but if your current belief is 70%, you should be as ready to drop it to 69% as raising it to 71%
content: Do the arithmetic on the essay's own example. A belief at 70% that can move only to 69% or 71% satisfies conservation of expected evidence only if 0.70 = p·0.71 + (1−p)·0.69, which gives p = ½. With equal step sizes the theorem requires equal readiness, so the essay's sentence is the theorem worked out for the case it chose. Fable's asymmetric pattern, frequent small rises and rare large falls, belongs to unequal step sizes, which the essay also allows: "Not every point may suffice to blow the issue wide open." The general statement Fable wants is the essay's next sentence: "You should not think that you know which direction it will go in (on average)." The essay states the mean-zero version and gives a correct worked instance of it.

quote: But you can’t produce curiosity just by willing it, any more than you can will your foot to feel warm when it feels cold.
content: "Just by willing it" is the operative phrase, and Loewenstein agrees. Curiosity does not come from willing. It comes from procedures that expose a gap, and the essay goes on to offer procedures. Fable grants that the essay's procedure is "precisely a gap-creating procedure." The theorem also explains why it works. Curiosity is an inverted-U function of confidence, highest when you are unsure of the answer and lowest when you are certain or clueless (Kang et al. 2009). Keeping each point of inquiry "evenly poised," with its direction genuinely unpredictable, holds you near the top of that curve. The theory and the practice fit, because the theory says where on the curve the practice puts you.
